name: Rafael Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a power line crew doing repairs and new connections for the electricity company. My technical diploma gave me the calculations, and years on the truck taught me to let the newest worker say when a reading looks wrong. I enjoy teaching that part; I dislike a callout arriving without the right pole number. My partner Nia and I have two children in school, a mortgage, higher pay than most lineworkers and about eight months of expenses saved. I use AI occasionally to tidy a handover note, then check it against the meter sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that a shorter handover note is useful if the switch number and meter reading stay visible. The actual repair still belongs to the person at the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This small change would not threaten my shifts or our mortgage. I do not want an apprentice to assume a clean AI summary means someone else verified the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the repair rota and add a box for the test reading to my handover template. In the first year I would ask the next shift which part of the new note still makes them ring back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little professional caution. The household can handle a paperwork experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the next shift ring back now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Usually the note says a fuse was replaced but leaves out the reading afterward. I would put the meter reading on the first line of the line repair handover, not bury it in a paragraph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a tool for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The company tool already does enough for my occasional use, and I see no reason to spend family money on a second one.

say: **AI handovers** help only when switch numbers and meter readings stay visible.
**Physical repair** still belongs to a lineworker at the site.
think: Our **eight-month buffer** and steady shifts keep the mortgage secure here.
An **apprentice** might mistake a clean summary for a verified repair.
do: **Keep** the repair rota and add a test-reading box to handovers.
**Ask** the next shift which missing details still cause a callback.
S0.quote: I would put the meter reading on the first line of the line repair handover, not bury it in a paragraph.
fieldNote: He uses **AI occasionally** and checks each handover against the meter sheet.
His **strong buffer** makes this a workmanship question rather than an income threat.

steps.text: Keep line repair rota and put test readings on handovers
Improve AI handover template using next-shift callbacks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a faster call desk could help us, but the new route plan needs a trial in a bucket truck. Thinking tasks change now; field robots come more slowly, so I would not rewrite the crew size on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company may take office costs out and then expect more repairs from the same people. My own pay might hold because I lead difficult jobs, and there are other utilities nearby, but I would watch the time pressure on apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the route plan on a dozen mixed jobs, including storm calls, and log any access error. In the first year I would bring the results to the supervisor and ask for the apprentices to join a review of repair-time targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a schedule that looks clean but misses the hard jobs. I am not expecting a household pay crisis from this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as an access error?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the plan sends our truck under a low branch or across a bridge with a weight limit, I would record the detour. A car route is not a bucket-truck route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the plan works on most jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would recommend using it, with a manual check for the exceptions. A good tool still needs someone who knows the truck to mark the bad turn.

say: **Call desk AI** may help, but bucket-truck routes need a mixed-job trial.
**Field robots** spread more slowly than desk automation.
think: My **lead pay** may hold while pressure rises for apprentices.
Nearby **utility jobs** offer a fallback if targets become unreasonable.
do: **Test** route plans on twelve mixed line jobs.
**Review** access errors and repair targets with supervisor and apprentices.
feel: **Uneasy** about time pressure, without expecting a household income crisis.
S1.quote: A car route is not a bucket-truck route.
fieldNote: His **trial design** includes storm calls and difficult access, not just easy routes.
His **financial position** makes apprentice workload more salient than immediate loss of his own pay.

steps.text: Test AI route plans on twelve mixed line jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 could change dispatch and diagrams first. Robots able to do our hands-on repairs arrive about 2031, and the gap is time to test what those machines can really handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose some repair hours after 2031 even if I am one of the senior workers. Eight months saved and plenty of nearby utilities let us search carefully, but a high wage can be hard to replace when every employer is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to observe a field robot trial on an old overhead line and compare its safety record with our crew’s. In the first year after 2028 I would take a company-funded protection testing course if a real local opening is attached, then apply for that post before 2031 if its pay covers our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing a good wage, but not overwhelmed. I have choices if I start early and check the offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which robot failure would concern you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot that repairs the conductor but misses a damaged insulator nearby would concern me. I would ask who checks the whole span before the line is re-energised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the testing post pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia and I would compare the offer with the mortgage and school costs. We could accept somewhat less, but not if it meant drawing from savings every month.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch before field robots arrive around 2031.
**Whole-span checks** matter when robots repair one visible fault.
think: Some **repair hours** may go after 2031 despite senior skill.
Eight months saved and **local utilities** help, but equal pay is uncertain.
do: **Observe** an old-line robot trial and compare full-span checks.
**Take** funded protection training only for a real local opening.
**Apply** before 2031 if the post covers fixed bills.
feel: **Anxious** about replacing a good wage, with options to pursue.
S2.quote: A robot that repairs the conductor but misses a damaged insulator nearby would concern me.
fieldNote: His **robot test** focuses on the full span, not just the component a machine touches.
His **training and application** depend on a funded course, real local vacancy and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Observe robot trial on old overhead line
Take company-funded protection course if linked to local opening
Apply for local protection testing before 2031 if pay covers fixed bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us room to watch several trials before thinking AI arrives in 2031. The capable field robots arrive around 2034, so apprentices should learn to inspect a robot repair as carefully as a human one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might prefer a training and inspection role by then, but only if the utility publishes a wage and enough posts. With two children and a mortgage, a new robot-inspection badge means less than a stable payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training manager to run a practical robot-inspection trial and publish the results. If the company offers paid assessor training with a real local post at a bill-covering wage, I would complete it before 2031 and apply in the first year after 2031; I would stay on the line crew if the offer never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful rather than frightened. The extra years let me try the work before asking Nia to trust a change in our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practical trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice and I would inspect the same robot repair independently, then compare what each of us found. I would want the machine’s missed defects written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the union to join?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the trial becomes a company policy. I would ask our union branch to make sure the test results are shared with every crew.

say: **Apprentices** should learn to inspect robot repairs before 2034.
**Trial results** should be shared with all crews if the method becomes policy.
think: A **new badge** does not replace a stable bill-covering wage.
I may prefer **training and inspection** if real posts exist.
do: **Run** a practical robot-inspection trial with the training manager.
**Complete** paid assessor training if a local bill-covering post exists.
**Apply** after 2031 if trained; otherwise retain line shifts.
feel: **Watchful**, with time to try the work before moving.
S3.quote: With two children and a mortgage, a new robot-inspection badge means less than a stable payslip.
fieldNote: His **trial** compares an apprentice’s inspection with his own on the same repair.
His **role move** depends on paid training, a real local post and wages that cover bills.

steps.text: Run practical robot-inspection trial with training manager
Complete paid assessor training if local bill-covering post exists
Apply for assessor role after 2031 if trained
Ask union branch to share trial results if adopted as company policy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade would let us prepare crews gradually before thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots around 2039. I would keep teaching apprentices how to spot a fault that the drawing leaves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be fifty-three at the first date and might still want to work full time. Our mortgage may not be finished, but our savings and nearby jobs let me wait for a training role that pays properly instead of jumping at a vague promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repair shifts and review the mortgage with Nia every year. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for a local line-safety instructor role if its pay covers our bills, and I would help write crew exercises for checking robot repairs if the utility introduces them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the runway. Ten years lets me teach line crews what I know while I decide whether a safety instructor post suits the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the crew exercise test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put a wrong switch number in a sample robot report and ask the crew to find it on the diagram before touching any equipment. No live line would be used in the exercise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early if the role does not appear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not have a retirement date from this picture. I would check the actual mortgage balance and keep working while the repair job remains available.

say: **Crew exercises** can teach workers to check robot reports before 2039.
**Apprentice learning** still needs physical fault finding.
think: I may want **full-time work** beyond fifty-three.
Savings and **nearby jobs** let me wait for a properly paid role.
do: **Review** the mortgage with Nia yearly while leading repairs.
**Apply** for local line-safety instruction after 2036 only at bill-covering pay.
**Write** crew robot-check exercises if the utility introduces them.
feel: **Calm** about time to teach and choose.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me teach line crews what I know while I decide whether a safety instructor post suits the family.
fieldNote: He does not treat **age fifty-three** or robots as a reason to retire early.
His **instructor move** remains conditional on a local role and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and review mortgage with Nia yearly
Apply for local line-safety instruction after 2036 if pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable field robots could begin replacing repairs around 2031 before I have tested another role. A funded course with a real local protection job and clear full-span safety checks would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask about the handover after a robot repair. The next line crew needs the meter values and the defects the repair robot did not fix, in plain sight.

portrait: **Rafael Larsen**, 43, leads a power line crew and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He and partner Nia have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, high lineworker pay and about eight months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for handovers, adopting tools after practical trials show they help crews.
In **Steady Disruption**, he tests twelve routes and worries more about apprentice workload than an immediate pay loss.
The **2028 scenario** worries him most because equal senior wages may be hard to find after field robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives him little time to secure another bill-covering role before field robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A funded **protection course** tied to a genuine local vacancy would make a job move possible.
Clear **whole-span checks** would keep robot repairs from hiding nearby defects.
headlineQuote: The next line crew needs the meter values and the defects the repair robot did not fix, in plain sight.
